verdict.reasoning: The patient opens with having “troubles… basically… I think it's diarrhea… super watery… just pouring straight from my bum,” indicating diarrhea as the chief complaint.

Duration: “it's been about three days now.” Frequency: “almost every hour I'm awake.” Character and no blood: “super watery… just fluids coming out” and when asked about blood, “No… there's nothing like that.”

Pain: “I feel a cramp and then I know it's time to go.” Location: “it's like at the bottom… it feels pretty like in the middle to me. Not on any side.” Intermittent: “It comes and goes.” Severity: patient estimates “maybe is that like a six or seven?”

Nausea/vomiting: “I definitely feel kind of nauseous… I have vomited.” Relation to milk: “whenever I have, like, milk… I just feel like I want to vomit… one time I… had some milk and I just completely vomited it.”

“I think I am pretty… I feel kind of really hot all the time… I haven't actually done any temperature reading… I'm not, like… Not a normal temperature,” indicating feeling febrile without measurement.
On urination: Doctor asks, “Are you passing urine? Okay.” Patient: “Yeah, but I guess less frequently maybe, but it seems to be okay,” which supports less frequent urination.
“My brother has had… something like this… for five days as well… I think he's getting better, but I'm not really sure,” supporting similar symptoms for 5 days and improvement.
“I've been taking some, like, paracetamols and stuff like that lately,” which supports that he is taking paracetamol.
Doctor: “I'll take it. You don't take any regular medications then?” Patient: “No… I haven't been, I'm not on any regular medication or anything like that.”
Doctor: “And do you have any allergies to any medications?” Patient: “So I don't have any allergies that I know of,” consistent with no known drug allergies.
Patient states, “My dad actually has colon cancer at the moment… he's sort of in his third stage,” supporting father with stage 3 colon cancer.
Work: “I work at an office in central London. It's… I work in government.” Home: “I live with my um, sister and my mum.”

Smoking: “I smoke for like socially but not like regularly.” Alcohol: “I might have a beer during the weekdays… maybe once or twice a month… we'll drink a lot,” which fits social smoking and occasional alcohol use.

“I just haven't really… I don't normally actually eat with my family… I haven't really gone into detail with my sister, my mom about it. Yeah. I just rather deal with these things,” indicating avoidance of discussing symptoms with family.
Doctor: “your symptoms are suggestive of something called gastroenteritis. A bit of a basic infection of your tummy,” making gastroenteritis the primary assessment.
Assessment is directly linked to history: doctor references symptoms of “pain and diarrhea” and earlier details of 3 days of watery, hourly diarrhea and cramps when concluding gastroenteritis.

The overall assessment of gastroenteritis is made in the context of diarrhea plus “nauseous… I have vomited,” with vomiting worsened by milk; this supports inclusion of nausea/vomiting in the gastroenteritis picture, with a possible lactose relationship.
The transcript notes the brother has similar symptoms but the doctor never explicitly states it is viral or names a suspected viral cause.
Doctor: “Make sure. You drink plenty of fluids… you can get things like diurelite, which is a fluid replacement we can get from the pharmacy. It's probably worth recommending that.”
Doctor: “clear fluids you can use soft diet, things like soup, mash, and then gradually build up as much as your body can tolerate.”
Doctor: “You can try just, you know, regular paracetamol if you are feeling feverish… If you've got bit of tummy pain… then I think paracetamol is very sensible.”
Doctor: “Try and avoid alcohol if you can.”
Doctor: “if your symptoms aren't settling down in the next couple of days, so 48 hours, I want you to give me a call back,” which is follow-up advice if symptoms persist beyond 48 hours.
The consultation is remote and contains no examination or vitals; no objective findings (e.g., physical exam, measured temperature, labs) are documented anywhere in the transcript.
